catalog_quote: § 6. Die Betonung. Die Grundregel für die Betonung im Bantu ist eine sehr einfache: Gewöhnlich ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe. Eine Art Nebenton entsteht durch einen langen Vokal, wenn er vor der Tonsilbe vorkommt: walĕhénda daß sie nicht gehen werden; ndžĕkápa ich werde schlagen; wŏlóka sie steigen nieder. Im Motschi zeigt sich die Tendenz, Bildungssuffixe, sofern sie nicht durch einen Konsonanten gestützt sind, zu enttonen zugunsten der Stammsilbe. ... Und Betonungen von Kausativen wie: wávĭṛa Wehe bereiten ...; -sahĭṛa kosten lassen (-saha kosten, osáhĭṛo der Bissen zum Kosten); -támŭṛa in Erinnerung bringen ... zeigen, daß selbst Bildungssuffixe, die einen Konsonanten als Stütze haben, enttont werden können. ... Oder sie bilden, wenn das vorhergehende Wort mehrsilbig ist, mit diesem in der Weise eine Toneinheit, daß der Ton des vorhergehenden Wortes auf die letzte Silbe rückt, werden also enklitisch. Beispiele: kapa-mbe schlage die Rinder! [Raum 1909: 36-37] || Le chaga (de même que des langues voisines, comme le kamba) est une langue où jouent en même temps un système tonal entièrement distinctif et un système d'accent démarcatif, les effets des deux s'entrecroisant. ... certains nominaux sortent du stade lexical avec une syllabe accentuée (soit la pénultième, soit la finale) et tous les tons B. [fn. 1] JC. Winter a ausi mis en lumière cette dualité dans le dialecte mochi, dans un article malheureusement trop bref (Winter, 1987) [Philippson 1991: 288]

sweep_summary: Mochi (moch1256) is not in the catalog. Three works with stress in the title, two of which are the same article. (1) Philippson 1991 doctoral thesis: NOT paywalled after all — the full 542-page PDF is open on the author's lab site (http://www.ddl.cnrs.fr/Fulltext/philippson/these.pdf,HTTP only), downloaded and read; Chaga (Vunjo data from McHugh 1990, Mochi via Winter 1987 and Nurse & Philippson 1977) is described as a two-tone language with a demarcative accent on the stem penultimate (final in monosyllables and ua>o contractions, a few unaccented ethnonyms), realised only group-finally and interacting with tone to produce super-high tones (pp. 288-289, 385-387, 483, 485). (2)=(3) Winter 1987 'Zur Prosodologie des Mochi-Dialekts des Chagga', AAP 12: 5-15 (Glottolog 176958 and 15979 are duplicate records): no open full text found (Cologne institute site and the Internet Archive unreachable, HathiTrust 403), but Google Books snippet view of the AAP 1987 volume plus the LLBA 1988 abstract were chained into a partial reconstruction: Winter rejects the two-tone analysis and posits three distinctive prosodemes, each a Druckakzent (stress accent) bundled with a pitch interval; noun stems carry DPI or DPII on the first stem syllable, other syllables DP0. This is the best Mochi-specific modern statement and remains HIGH priority to acquire in print. Previously held by the project (prior check): Raum 1909 §6 'Die Betonung' (penultimate 'Ton', enclisis shifts it) — page scan pp. 36-37 verified by eye this search of works with stress in the title; Nurse & Philippson 1977 (tone only, silent on stress); Salone 1980; Moshi & Ismail 2022 (no stress statement). all lookups went through bibliographic APIs, theses.fr, HAL, Google Books feed API and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: § 6. Die Betonung. Die Grundregel für die Betonung im Bantu ist eine sehr einfache: Gewöhnlich ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe. Eine Art Nebenton entsteht durch einen langen Vokal, wenn er vor der Tonsilbe vorkommt: walēhénda daß sie nicht gehen werden; ndžēkápa ich werde schlagen; wōlóka sie steigen nieder. Im Motschi zeigt sich die Tendenz, Bildungssuffixe, sofern sie nicht durch einen Konsonanten gestützt sind, zu enttonen zugunsten der Stammsilbe. [...] Oder sie [einsilbige Wörter] bilden, wenn das vorhergehende Wort mehrsilbig ist, mit diesem in der Weise eine Toneinheit, daß der Ton des vorhergehenden Wortes auf die letzte Silbe rückt, werden also enklitisch. Beispiele: kapa-mbe schlage die Rinder!
new_statements.translation: §6. Accentuation. The basic rule for accentuation in Bantu is a very simple one: ordinarily the accent rests on the penultimate syllable. A kind of secondary accent arises from a long vowel when it occurs before the tonic syllable: walēhénda 'that they will not go'; ndžēkápa 'I shall strike'; wōlóka 'they climb down'. In Mochi there is a tendency to de-accent derivational suffixes, insofar as they are not supported by a consonant, in favour of the stem syllable. [...] Or, when the preceding word is polysyllabic, they [monosyllabic words] form an accent unit with it in such a way that the accent of the preceding word moves to its last syllable, i.e. they become enclitic. Examples: kapa-mbé 'strike the cattle!'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the penultimate syllable; a monosyllabic word following a polysyllabic one encliticises, so the accent moves to the host's final syllable (= penult of the accent group). Raum treats lexical/grammatical pitch ('Intonation', three tone levels, minimal pairs) as a separate system in §7; modern analyses (Nurse & Philippson 1977, Saloné 1980) describe Old Moshi as a two-tone (H/L) language and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Eine Art Nebenton' (a kind of secondary accent) on a long vowel preceding the tonic syllable (walēhénda, ndžēkápa, wōlóka).
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel-only derivational suffixes (-ia/-ea > -ya etc.) are de-accented in favour of the stem syllable, and some causatives (wáviŗa, -sahíŗa, -támuŗa) show accent retracted off the suffix; the monosyllabic genitive particle keeps its own accent (mburu ja mka) except before a verb; enclitic demonstratives lose initial i-; adverbial enclitic suffixes (-se, -nu, -fo) do NOT move the verb's tonic syllable (átša-se, hénda-nu, ngakúnda-se-fo); monosyllables with a long final vowel (ndzā, mō, mī, -kā) 'hold the tone' and cannot become enclitic.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word, extended to the 'Toneinheit' (accent group = polysyllabic host + monosyllabic enclitic, or two words contracted across a vowel hiatus in rapid speech). Author frames the rule as the general Bantu rule applying to Mochi ('Motschi'); 1909 missionary grammar, impressionistic, no instrumental basis. Contrastive pitch is handled separately (§7), so the language is tonal-with-a-stress-statement in modern terms; the later tonal literature on Old Moshi does not discuss stress at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Raum 1909 describes the 'Moschi-Dialekt' ('Motschi'), i.e. Old Moshi Chaga = Kimochi = Glottolog moch1256 (ISO old), Central Kilimanjaro group; Nurse & Philippson 1977 and Saloné 1980 likewise treat 'Old Moshi (kimoci)'. Not to be confused with Vunjo (vunj1238, McHugh's KiVunjo) or Machame (mach1266). Mallya 2018 (held) is Kibosho/Marangu, not Mochi.

new_statements.quote: "Pour chaque schème tonal (BB, HB, BH, HH et aussi HBB ...), on peut opposer thèmes accentués sur la pénultième, sur la finale, ou non-accentués. La première catégorie est de loin la plus nombreuse, la deuxième comprend essentiellement les thèmes monosyllabiques ou ceux issus d'une contraction; cf. les verbo-nominaux au passif : [...] L'accent est sur la pénultième du thème dans les deux cas, mais le processus de coalescence vocalique ua > o, qui s'applique sans exception dans les dialectes chaga du centre aboutit finalement à accentuer la finale."
new_statements.translation: For each tone pattern (LL, HL, LH, HH and also HLL ...), one can oppose stems accented on the penultimate, on the final, or unaccented. The first category is by far the most numerous; the second comprises essentially monosyllabic stems or those resulting from a contraction; cf. the passive verbo-nominals: [...] The accent is on the penultimate of the stem in both cases, but the vowel-coalescence process ua > o, which applies without exception in the central Chaga dialects, ends up accenting the final.
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard (1991). Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de Doctorat d'Etat, Université Paris V.
new_statements.locator: pp. 385-386 (Ch. 5 §3.12.3.1, Chaga; Vunjo data after McHugh 1990, extended to Mochi at p. 288 fn. 1 via Winter 1987); see also p. 288-289 and p. 485
new_statements.reading: Chaga of Kilimanjaro, including the central dialects Vunjo and Mochi, has a demarcative accent superimposed on a fully distinctive two-tone system: the accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem in the great majority of stems, on the final in monosyllabic stems and in stems whose final vowel is the product of ua>o coalescence (passives, some place/ethnic names), and is absent in a small class of ethnonyms; it is realised only at the end of a prosodic group (neutralised group-internally) and its interaction with tone yields super-high tones. For Mochi specifically Philippson credits Winter 1987 with demonstrating the same tone/accent duality (p. 288 fn. 1); Winter's own snippet-visible formulation places a stress accent (Druckakzent) with a pitch interval on the first stem syllable of nouns, which coincides with the penultimate for the disyllabic stems that dominate the lexicon. The oldest first-hand Mochi grammar, Raum 1909 §6 p. 36 (already held by the project; page scan checked by eye this search of works with stress in the title), states 'Gewöhnlich ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe' with enclitics shifting the accent to the host's last syllable. Catalog-wise: penultimate (stem) stress with lexically fixed final exceptions, coexisting with lexical tone; not a purely positional stress language.

new_statements.quote: Der Mochi-Dialekt hat die folgenden drei distinktiven Prosodeme (kurz DP): 1. Das DPI besteht aus einem Druckakzent und einem zur nächstfolgenden Silbe absteigenden Ton-Intervall; ich markiere es mit einem Tiefton-Zeichen (accent [grave]) ... 2. Das DPII besteht aus einem zur nächstfolgenden Silbe aufsteigenden Ton-Intervall und einem Druckakzent auf dieser ... Hochton-Zeichen (accent aigu) auf dem sonoren Element ebendieser nächstfolgenden Silbe. ... 3. Das DP0 besitzt keine eigenen Druckakzent- oder Tonintervallcharakteristika ... [Nomina im] Mochi gliedern sich in zwei Klassen: diejenigen mit einem DPI und diejenigen mit einem DPII auf der ersten Stammsilbe. Weitere Silben, soweit vorhanden, tragen DP0s.
new_statements.translation: The Mochi dialect has the following three distinctive prosodemes (DP): 1. DPI consists of a stress accent (Druckakzent) and a pitch interval falling to the next syllable; I mark it with a low-tone sign (grave accent) ... 2. DPII consists of a pitch interval rising to the next syllable and a stress accent on that [next] syllable ... high-tone sign (acute) on the sonorant element of that next syllable. ... 3. DP0 has no stress or pitch-interval characteristics of its own ... [Nouns in] Mochi fall into two classes: those with a DPI and those with a DPII on the first stem syllable. Further syllables, where present, carry DP0s.
new_statements.citation: Winter, J.C. (1987). Zur Prosodie des Mochi-Dialekts des Chagga. Afrikanistische Arbeitspapiere 12: 5-16. [Glottolog 176958, Zurich catalogue record; same article as Glottolog 15979 — correct title 'Zur Prosodologie.', pp. 5-15 per Anthropos 1988 and LLBA 1988]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with Philippson 1991 (who cites this article at p. 288 fn. 1 as showing the same tone/accent duality as Vunjo) and with Raum 1909 on the stem-initial/penultimate location of the DPI stress in the dominant disyllabic stems; but it makes the stressed syllable depend on the lexical prosodeme class (DPII stems stress the second stem syllable), so it complicates the plain 'penultimate' rule recorded from Raum. Only snippets read; Cologne institute hosts unreachable (automated download rc=7); no archive.org or HathiTrust copy.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prosody is a set of lexically chosen 'prosodemes' each bundling a stress accent (Druckakzent) with a pitch interval; every noun stem carries DPI or DPII on its first stem syllable and DP0 elsewhere. Under DPI the stress sits on the first stem syllable (penult of a disyllabic stem); under DPII the stress sits on the syllable after it (final of a disyllabic stem). Stress position is thus fixed relative to the stem but its exact syllable depends on the lexical prosodeme class; it is not an independent contrastive stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated in the snippets. Winter says DPIs in certain word classes and syntactic positions are realised by their stress accent alone (without the falling interval), and in the compilation of three DPIs the middle one also loses its stress accent (c. p. 9).
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns having only DPI (plus DP0) get a DPII on the class prefix (c. p. 9). Sequences of DPII are realised as a rising sequence; realisation rules for DPI+DPII sequences at c. p. 11. Winter contests the two-tone (H/L) analysis of Nurse & Philippson 1977 and argues the prosodeme is not confined to one syllable (LLBA 1988 abstract).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Mochi (Motschi, Old Moshi) dialect of Kilimanjaro Chaga specifically: Raum's grammar is titled 'Moschi-Dialekt' and Winter's article 'Mochi-Dialekt'. Winter's opening pages also discuss the Machame dialect (Sharp 1954, nine tone categories) as a comparison; that material is not about Mochi. The existing Philippson 1991 statement is built on Vunjo data (McHugh 1990) and extended to Mochi via Winter 1987.

new_statements.quote: Die Grundregel für die Betonung im Bantu ist eine sehr einfache: Gewöhnlich ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe. Eine Art Nebenton entsteht durch einen langen Vokal, wenn er vor der Tonsilbe vorkommt: walĕhénda daß sie nicht gehen werden; ndžĕkápa ich werde schlagen; wŏlóka sie steigen nieder. [p. 36-37] ... Oder sie bilden, wenn das vorhergehende Wort mehrsilbig ist, mit diesem in der Weise eine Toneinheit, daß der Ton des vorhergehenden Wortes auf die letzte Silbe rückt, werden also enklitisch. Beispiele: kapa-mbe schlage die Rinder!; šinga-mba schließe das Haus [p. 37] ... Enklitisch sind ferner die adverbialen Suffixe; selbst wenn mehrere hintereinander stehen, wird die Tonsilbe des vorangehenden Zeitwortes nicht verrückt: átša-se er kommt wieder [p. 37]
new_statements.translation: The basic rule for stress in Bantu is a very simple one: usually the stress rests on the penultimate syllable. A kind of secondary stress arises from a long vowel when it occurs before the stressed syllable: walĕhénda 'that they will not go'; ndžĕkápa 'I shall strike'; wŏlóka 'they climb down'. ... Or, when the preceding word is polysyllabic, they form a stress unit with it in such a way that the stress of the preceding word moves to its last syllable, i.e. they become enclitic. Examples: kapa-mbe 'strike the cattle!'; šinga-mba 'shut the house' ... Adverbial suffixes are also enclitic; even when several follow one another, the stressed syllable of the preceding verb is not shifted: átša-se 'he comes again'. (The diacritic on the pre-tonic vowel in the three examples is not resolvable at scan resolution; the text calls it a long vowel.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress ('Ton' in Raum's terminology, distinguished from pitch = 'Intonation') normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. A monosyllabic enclitic (noun, demonstrative) shifts the host's stress to the host's final syllable, i.e. penultimate of the clitic group; adverbial suffixes (-se, -fo, -nu) do not shift it. Long-voweled monosyllables keep their own stress and cannot become enclitic (p. 36). Derivational suffixes tend to be destressed in favour of the stem syllable (p. 37), giving antepenultimate stress in some causatives (wáviŗa, -sahíŗa, -támuŗa).
new_statements.secondary_stress: A kind of secondary stress ('eine Art Nebenton') on a long vowel preceding the stressed syllable (p. 36-37).
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitic monosyllables shift stress to the host's final syllable; the genitive particle keeps its own stress except before a verb; causatives and other derived verbs may stress the stem syllable rather than the penult (-sahíŗa, -támuŗa); contracted word pairs and semivocalised junctures form one stress unit (pp. 37-38). § 7 (pp. 38-40) states separately that Mochi distinguishes three pitch levels (high, mid, low) that differentiate otherwise identical words, i.e. the language is tonal.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Mochi (Motschi, Old Moshi) dialect of Kilimanjaro Chaga specifically: Raum's grammar is titled 'Moschi-Dialekt' and Winter's article 'Mochi-Dialekt'. Winter's opening pages also discuss the Machame dialect (Sharp 1954, nine tone categories) as a comparison; that material is not about Mochi. The existing Philippson 1991 statement is built on Vunjo data (McHugh 1990) and extended to Mochi via Winter 1987.

readall_conflicts: Raum 1909 (§ 6, pp. 36-37) states a positional rule: stress usually on the penultimate syllable, with enclitics shifting it to the host's final syllable and some derived verbs stressing the stem syllable; tone is treated separately as three pitch levels (§ 7). Winter 1987 (snippets only, c. pp. 8-9) does not give a positional stress rule; it folds the stress accent (Druckakzent) into lexically selected prosodemes on the first stem syllable, so that a DPI noun stem is stressed on its first stem syllable (penult of a disyllable) while a DPII stem is stressed on the syllable after it (final of a disyllable). For the dominant disyllabic DPI stems this coincides with Raum's penult; for DPII stems it does not. Philippson 1991 (existing statement, pp. 385-386, 288 fn. 1) reconciles the two: a demarcative penultimate-stem accent with a lexically fixed final-accent class, superimposed on lexical tone. Winter also explicitly contests the two-tone (H/L) analysis of Nurse & Philippson 1977. So the sources disagree on the analysis of the prosodic system, not on the surface fact that most words are prominent on the penultimate/first stem syllable. On the snippet evidence Winter 1987 does not contradict the catalog's Raum 1909 penultimate rule for the dominant disyllabic stems (DPI = stress on the first stem syllable = penult), but it ties the stressed syllable to a lexical prosodeme class (DPII stresses the syllable after the first stem syllable) inside a tone system, which sides with Phi…

[...] Oder sie [einsilbige Wörter] bilden, wenn das vorhergehende Wort mehrsilbig ist, mit diesem in der Weise eine Toneinheit, daß der Ton des vorhergehenden Wortes auf die letzte Silbe rückt, werden also enklitisch. Beispiele: kapa-mbe schlage die Rinder!

sources.note: §6 'Die Betonung' (pp.36-38): the tone/stress ordinarily rests on the penultimate syllable; a kind of secondary accent arises on a long vowel before the tonic syllable; derivational suffixes tend to be de-accented in favour of the stem syllable; monosyllabic words encliticise to the preceding word so that its accent moves to its last syllable (i.e. penult of the accent unit), except the genitive particle; adverbial enclitic suffixes do NOT shift the verb's tonic syllable. §7 'Die Intonation' (pp.38-40) separately says pitch distinguishes otherwise identical words and posits three tones (high,…

sources.quote: "Der Mochi-Dialekt hat die folgenden drei distinktiven Prosodeme (kurz DP): 1. Das DPI besteht aus einem Druckakzent und einem zur nächstfolgenden Silbe absteigenden Ton-Intervall; ich markiere es mit einem Tiefton-Zeichen (accent [grave]) ... 2. Das DPII besteht aus einem zur nächstfolgenden Silbe aufsteigenden Ton-Intervall und einem Druckakzent auf dieser ... Hochton-Zeichen (accent aigu) auf dem sonoren Element ebendieser nächstfolgenden Silbe. ... 3. Das DP0 besitzt keine eigenen Druckakzent- oder Tonintervallcharakteristika ... [Nomina im] Mochi gliedern sich in zwei Klassen: diejenigen mit einem DPI und diejenigen mit einem DPII auf der ersten Stammsilbe. Weitere Silben, soweit vorhanden, tragen DP0s."

sources.note: Snippet-only reconstruction (no full text read). Winter rejects the two-tone (H/L) analysis of Nurse & Philippson 1977 and describes Mochi word prosody as three distinctive 'prosodemes', each bundling a stress accent (Druckakzent) with a pitch interval to the next syllable: DPI = stress + falling interval (marked grave), DPII = rising interval + stress on the following syllable (marked acute), DP0 = no stress/interval of its own. sources.quote: Die Grundregel für die Betonung im Bantu ist eine sehr einfache: Gewöhnlich ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe. Eine Art Nebenton entsteht durch einen langen Vokal, wenn er vor der Tonsilbe vorkommt: walĕhénda daß sie nicht gehen werden; ndžĕkápa ich werde schlagen; wŏlóka sie steigen nieder. [p. 36-37] ... Oder sie bilden, wenn das vorhergehende Wort mehrsilbig ist, mit diesem in der Weise eine Toneinheit, daß der Ton des vorhergehenden Wortes auf die letzte Silbe rückt, werden also enklitisch. Beispiele: kapa-mbe schlage die Rinder!; šinga-mba schließe das Haus [p. 37] ... Enklitisch sind ferner die adverbialen Suffixe; selbst wenn mehrere hintereinander stehen, wird die Tonsilbe des vorangehenden Zeitwortes nicht verrückt: átša-se er kommt wieder [p. 37]
